tldr: We propose DQ-MPCC, a novel MPCC that unifies position and attitude using unit dual quaternions in the body frame; deployed directly to real-world racing with the exact same gains from simulation, it achieved 10.5% faster lap times than the baseline while strictly respecting gate passage margins.
hero_caption: Racing flight on an eight-gate real-world circuit (top) and quadrotor center position plots at each gate crossing (bottom). The proposed DQ-MPCC (red squares) stays within the geometric safety margin (green dashed line) across all gates, whereas the conventional baseline MPCC (blue circles) exceeds the safety boundary at gate 2 (G2) and elsewhere.
overview:
Autonomous drone racing is an extreme control challenge requiring quadrotors to pass through narrow gates at maximum speed. In this domain, Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC)—which optimizes spatial progress online without fixing time allocation—has become a standard tool. However, conventional MPCC formulations describe translational motion (position) in the inertial frame and rotational motion (attitude) in the body frame. This split tends to distort predictive model linearizations and error metrics during aggressive maneuvers where translation and rotation are strongly coupled.

To address this, the authors turned to unit dual quaternions, which unify position and attitude within a single mathematical framework. They formulated the rigid-body equations of motion using dual quaternions and dual twists (linear plus angular velocities) entirely in the body frame. Furthermore, tracking errors are projected onto the tangent space of the dual quaternion manifold (the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{se}(3)$) expressed in the desired body frame and orthogonally decomposed into lag error and contouring error, resulting in DQ-MPCC.

Evaluation was conducted using a MuJoCo-based Software-in-the-Loop (SiL) environment and an 8-gate 3D racing circuit ($11\times 4.5\times 3.65$ m) in the real world. Control gains tuned via multi-objective Bayesian optimization in simulation were transferred directly to hardware without any retuning. Due to the Sim-to-Real gap, the baseline MPCC suffered a 71.5% increase in worst-gate crossing error compared to simulation and violated the safety margin. In contrast, DQ-MPCC reduced its worst-gate error by 10.1%, reliably keeping all crossings within the safe margin. It also reduced the real-world lap time by 10.5% while running onboard in real time at 100 Hz.
contributions: Formulation of DQ-MPCC for drone racing using unit dual quaternions that unify position, attitude, linear velocity, and angular velocity in the body frame
Design of a tracking cost that projects errors onto the dual quaternion tangent space $\mathfrak{se}(3)$ in the desired body frame, cleanly separating and penalizing lag and contouring errors
Demonstration in SiL simulations that, among configurations satisfying safety margins, DQ-MPCC cuts lap times by 6.7% over the conventional MPCC through rigorous multi-objective search
Zero-shot deployment to physical hardware without gain retuning, maintaining the geometric safety margin across all gates while reducing real-world lap times by 10.5%

sections.heading: Why does the choice of coordinate frames matter in drone racing?
sections.summary: Drone racing demands extreme agility, creating strong coupling between translation and rotation. Conventional MPCC handles inertial position and body attitude separately, but this paper proposes DQ-MPCC to treat rigid-body motion uniformly on a manifold using dual quaternions.
sections.details:
Achieving minimum-time flight in drone racing requires flying at extreme attitude limits (aggressive roll and pitch angles) while precisely traversing narrow gates. Recently, Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) has gained popularity because it optimizes progress along a spatial path as a decision variable rather than using fixed time stamps.

However, most existing drone MPCC formulations (including state-of-the-art methods like MPCC++) express translational contouring errors in the inertial frame and attitude errors in the body frame. During high-G maneuvers with steep tilts, correcting even a tiny inertial position error requires rapid attitude changes. Consequently, position and attitude control objectives strongly interfere with each other right at critical gate crossings.

This is where unit dual quaternions come in. Dual quaternions represent 3D rigid-body position and attitude within a single algebraic system, and their logarithmic map unfolds motion errors directly onto the tangent space of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{se}(3)$. The authors introduced this approach into MPCC to separate lag error (along the path) and contouring error (transverse to the path) in the desired body frame. Running at 100 Hz onboard a Jetson Orin NX, it exhibits remarkable robustness during Sim-to-Real transfer compared to the inertial-frame baseline.

DQ-MPCC (red) consistently clusters within the safe clearance region (green dashed line), whereas the baseline MPCC (blue) drifts significantly outward, particularly at gate G2.

sections.heading: Unifying quadrotor dynamics with dual quaternions
sections.summary: Combining quaternions with the dual number unit, the authors derive an elegant equation of motion describing quadrotor position, attitude, velocity, and angular velocity in a body-fixed frame.
sections.details:
### II-A Dual Quaternion Algebra Recap
A dual quaternion $\hat{\bm{q}}=\bm{q}_{p}+\varepsilon\,\bm{q}_{d}$ combines two quaternions—primal and dual parts—linked by the dual unit $\varepsilon$ where $\varepsilon^2=0$ (with $\varepsilon\neq 0$). Defining a unit dual quaternion $\hat{\bm{q}} = \bm{q}_r + \varepsilon\,\tfrac{1}{2}\bm{p}\otimes\bm{q}_r$ from an attitude unit quaternion $\bm{q}_r$ and a position vector $\bm{p}$ (a pure quaternion) yields a double cover of the rigid-body transformation group $SE(3)$. This allows position and attitude to be handled seamlessly together.

### II-B Standard Quadrotor Motion Model
This work uses a body-rate input interface where a low-level angular rate controller (INDI) tracks rate commands $\bm{\omega}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$ via a first-order lag with time constant $\tau_{rc}$. The control input is a 4D vector $\bm{u}=[f, \bm{\omega}_{\mathrm{cmd}}^\top]^\top$ consisting of total collective thrust $f$ and angular rate commands $\bm{\omega}_{\mathrm{cmd}}$.

### II-C Dual Quaternion Quadrotor Dynamics
Combining body-frame linear velocity $\bm{v}_b = \bm{R}^\top(\bm{q}_r)\bm{v}$ and angular velocity $\bm{\omega}$ into a pure dual quaternion yields the dual twist $\hat{\bm{\xi}} = \bm{\omega} + \varepsilon\,\bm{v}_b$. Using this, the position and attitude kinematics simplify to the compact product $\dot{\hat{\bm{q}}} = \tfrac{1}{2}\hat{\bm{q}}\boxtimes\hat{\bm{\xi}}$. Furthermore, velocity and acceleration dynamics are formulated as derivatives of the dual twist entirely within the body frame, resulting in a fully unified representation of nonlinear rigid-body dynamics.

sections.heading: Three-stage reference path generation for boundary racing
sections.summary: A smooth geometric reference path pipeline solves an offline point-mass minimum-time problem from gate layouts and lifts it to a 3D trajectory and attitude profile via differential flatness.
sections.details:
In MPCC, the progress speed $v_s = \dot{s}$ along the arc length $s$ of a spatial path is determined online subject to vehicle constraints. High-quality offline reference paths are therefore essential. The authors generate these paths in three stages:

- ### Gate Layout
Eight gates are arranged in an $11\times 4.5\times 3.65$ m volume. The gate opening radius is $R_{\rm gate}=0.50$ m, which yields a geometric safety clearance of $R_{\rm safe}=0.30$ m after subtracting the drone's propeller radius $r_{\rm drone}=0.20$ m.

- ### Point-Mass Minimum-Time Lap Planning
First, a point-mass model (PMM) is used to solve an offline periodic minimum-time optimal control problem (OCP) requiring the vehicle to pass within 5 cm of each gate center. Maximum acceleration is deliberately set to $5g$, exceeding the drone's physical capability. Because MPCC optimizes speed online based on actuator limits, the geometric path merely needs to be smooth even if it is dynamically unfeasible as planned.

- ### Arc-Length Reparameterization and Flatness-Based Lifting
The resulting path is resampled by arc length $s$ and smoothed with a Gaussian filter. Quadrotor differential flatness is then used to derive the reference attitude quaternion $\bm{q}_r^d(s)$ and body rates $\bm{\omega}_0(s)$ from the required thrust direction. These are encoded as B-splines and evaluated inside the online optimization.

sections.heading: Controller design: decomposing errors on the manifold tangent space
sections.summary: Dual quaternion errors are mapped via the logarithmic map onto the $\mathfrak{se}(3)$ tangent space and decomposed into lag and contouring errors in the desired body frame. Approximating the inverse left Jacobian enables 100 Hz real-time optimization.
sections.details:
### IV-A & IV-B Augmented State and OCP
The augmented state incorporates dual quaternion states, progress variables $(s, v_s)$, and a thrust state $f$ for rate limiting. The prediction horizon $T_p$ is split into $N$ intervals using a non-uniform grid that clusters stages near the current state, and the resulting nonlinear OCP discretized via ERK4 is solved at each step.

### IV-C & IV-D Dual Quaternion Pose Error and Logarithmic Map
The discrepancy between current pose $\hat{\bm{q}}$ and reference pose $\hat{\bm{q}}^d(s)$ is defined as the left-invariant pose error $\hat{\bm{q}}^e = \hat{\bm{q}}^{d*}\boxtimes\hat{\bm{q}}$, expressed in the desired body frame. Applying the logarithmic map onto the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{se}(3)$ yields rotational error coordinates $\bm{\phi}^e$ and translational error coordinates $\bm{\rho}^e$.

While exact translational mapping involves the inverse left Jacobian of $SO(3)$, $\bm{J}_l^{-1}$, the onboard implementation uses an identity approximation $\bm{J}_l^{-1} \approx \bm{I}$ near small rotational errors, giving $\bm{\rho}^e = \bm{R}^{d\top}(\bm{p}-\bm{p}^d)$ and significantly reducing computational load.

### IV-E & IV-F Error Decomposition and Constraints
Projecting $\bm{\rho}^e$ onto the path tangent $\bm{t}^d_b$ in the desired body frame provides an orthogonal decomposition into lag error $\bm{\rho}_{\mathrm{lag}}$ (along track) and contouring error $\bm{\rho}_{\mathrm{cont}}$ (cross track). The stage cost weights these against rotational error $\bm{\phi}^e$, progress reward, and input rate penalties.
Additionally, variable tube constraints $d_{\mathrm{tube}}(s)$—narrow near gates and relaxed in between—as well as actuator bounds are enforced as soft inequality constraints with slack variables.

sections.heading: Rigorous multi-objective auto-tuning for fair comparison
sections.summary: Using acados and SQP-RTI at 100 Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, control gains were tuned fairly under identical safety criteria via multi-objective Bayesian optimization using Optuna and NSGA-III.
sections.details:
### Numerical Implementation and Baseline Design
The real-time nonlinear MPC solver `acados` was used with SQP-RTI (Real-Time Iteration). To ensure a fair comparison, the baseline MPCC was built with the exact same solver, horizon, constraints, reference path, actuator limits, and cost structure. The only difference is state representation (inertial position/velocity with quaternions) and traditional error decomposition in the static inertial frame $\mathbb{R}^3 \times \mathfrak{so}(3)$.

### V-A Gain Tuning via Multi-Objective Optimization
To avoid relying on manual tuning heuristics, multi-objective optimization (NSGA-III with TPE) was conducted using Optuna. The objectives were minimizing lap time and minimizing worst-gate offset.

A strict criterion was enforced: any parameter set that violated the safety clearance $R_{\rm safe} = 30$ cm even once in simulation was disqualified. The fastest configuration among those remaining within the margin across all gates was selected. Baseline candidates that appeared faster than DQ-MPCC were discarded because they violated gate clearances.

sections.heading: Simulation results: 6.7% faster lap times and internal behavior analysis
sections.summary: In 100-seed Monte Carlo SiL simulations, DQ-MPCC achieved 6.7% faster lap times while maintaining safety constraints. Ablation studies confirmed the impact of the Jacobian approximation.
sections.details:
### Lap Time and Trajectory Comparison
In noisy 100-seed Monte Carlo SiL simulations, DQ-MPCC achieved a median lap time of $3.23$ s, a $6.7\%$ improvement over the baseline ($3.46$ s). Total path length was also $2.9\%$ shorter ($21.8$ m vs. $22.4$ m for the baseline), demonstrating tighter racing lines.

### Computational Load and Constraint Satisfaction
Because of the larger state dimension in the dual quaternion formulation, the per-step solve time increased by about $1.7$ ms compared to the baseline. Nonetheless, it averaged $5.9$ ms on the Jetson Orin NX, easily meeting the $10$ ms (100 Hz) loop deadline. Quaternion norm drift across the horizon was negligible.

### Exact Jacobian Ablation
The inverse left Jacobian approximation $\bm{J}_l^{-1} \approx \bm{I}$ was compared against the exact formulation with identical gains. Attitude errors averaged around $16^\circ$ during racing (exceeding $50^\circ$ at the 99th percentile), meaning Jacobian effects are present. While the exact Jacobian added $\approx 0.2$ ms of compute time, it further reduced lap time to $3.16$ s with zero collisions. The approximation remains fast and stable, but exact calculations present further optimization headroom.

sections.heading: Real-world flights: 10.5% faster without retuning and a Sim-to-Real turnaround
sections.summary: Flying on hardware with identical simulation gains revealed a stark contrast: the baseline frequently breached safety margins due to the Sim-to-Real gap, whereas DQ-MPCC stayed within margin at every gate and cut lap times by 10.5%.
sections.details:
### Real-World Flights and Sim-to-Real Transfer
Hardware experiments were conducted on a motion-capture circuit, completing 6 flights (18 laps) per controller in a zero-shot transfer without any gain retuning from simulation.

The results were striking. In the real world, DQ-MPCC achieved a minimum lap time of $3.14$ s compared to $3.51$ s for the baseline—a $10.5\%$ reduction. Gate-crossing accuracy was even more telling: while the baseline had smaller average errors in simulation, its worst-gate offset jumped by $+71.5\%$ ($30.7$ cm) on hardware, exceeding the safety clearance $R_{\rm safe} = 30$ cm in 4 out of 6 flights.

In contrast, DQ-MPCC's worst-gate offset actually improved to $22.1$ cm (a $10.1\%$ reduction relative to simulation), respecting safety clearances on every single flight and gate.

### What Caused This Discrepancy?
Hardware flight introduces communication latencies and model mismatches. Under these disturbances, the baseline suffered from cross-talk between attitude lags and inertial position errors; its 99th-percentile acceleration spiked by $+17.5\%$ ($34.9$ m/s$^2$) over simulation, causing excessive hunting and counter-steering. Conversely, DQ-MPCC unifies attitude and translation in the body frame, executing calm, consistent trajectory corrections without frantic actuator chattering. This coordinate representation proved decisive for Sim-to-Real robustness.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: Formulating quadrotor racing dynamics via dual quaternions in the body frame offers superior Sim-to-Real robustness and speed. Future work includes integrating onboard visual odometry.
sections.details:
This paper presented DQ-MPCC, combining unit dual quaternions in the body frame with Lie-algebraic contouring error decomposition for minimum-time quadrotor racing.

Its key achievement is unmatched Sim-to-Real transfer: using gains tuned purely in simulation, it respected safety margins 100% of the time while outperforming the baseline lap time by over 10%. Even when modeling the exact same physical system, the choice of coordinate frames and algebraic representations fundamentally alters SQP-RTI linearization properties and determines resilience against real-world delays and mismatches.

Future avenues noted by the authors include integrating onboard vision-based state estimation to replace motion capture, testing on larger outdoor tracks, and updating reference attitude profiles online based on real-time progress speed.

takeaways: Treating position and attitude together in the body frame via dual quaternions prevents control breakdown caused by translational-rotational coupling during high-G turns.

Even with identical physical models, coordinate choices (inertial vs. body-frame manifold representations) change SQP-RTI linearization behavior, creating a massive difference in Sim-to-Real robustness.
Enforcing strict geometric safety criteria during automated tuning ensures reliable, crash-free performance when deploying aggressively tuned policies to hardware.
limitations: State estimation relies on an external high-rate (240 Hz) motion capture system; resilience against biases and latency from onboard cameras and IMUs remains unverified.
Reference attitude profiles are derived from offline planning accelerations, leaving a potential attitude mismatch when online progress speed $v_s$ deviates from the nominal plan.
Real-world evaluations were limited to 6 completed flights (18 laps) per controller, which may not fully capture long-term drift or statistical outliers.
